title: The empire around 1000
hook: Saxon royal centres and Italian imperial coronation formed a geography spanning the Alps.
notes: Met Ottonian Art and UNESCO Quedlinburg. 1000 is a cultural-period snapshot. The map shows cited political/cultural centres, not speculative territory. Coordinates are approximate named-place locators, not imported surveyed points. Modern borders are hidden. Event cards contain claim-level citations. The later term Holy Roman Empire must not be projected unchanged onto Charlemagne’s Frankish realm.

scenes.title: Royal authority at Aachen
scenes.text: In 936 Otto became king at Aachen. A long-used ceremonial centre helped connect a new dynasty to earlier imperial memory.

scenes.title: Imperial authority at Rome
scenes.text: Otto received the imperial title in Rome in 962. Move the timeline: Aachen’s royal anchor remains while the Roman imperial connection enters the map.

scenes.title: Saxon centres
scenes.text: Quedlinburg belonged to the heartland of Saxon-Ottonian rulership. Around 1000, royal places and religious communities helped sustain government; this city anchor does not define an imperial border.

scenes.title: Churches and imperial culture
scenes.text: Hildesheim’s bronze monuments drew on ancient imperial and early Christian models. Compare this ecclesiastical centre with Quedlinburg in the previous scene: churches and royal sites sustained different parts of the northern imperial world.
